turn_text: It's outrageous that a congressperson, a congressman for the most part that I know of, can treat a staff member the way that it's coming out that congressmen have done that sexually inappropriate contact. And then in order to get out of the jam, pay the person off, but pay the person off using tax dollars. That money should come out of the congressman's personal pocket, not the taxpayer, and plus the fact that that congressman person needs to be investigated. My legislation simply says it comes out of their pocket. We're making it retroactive that the congressman's name will be published. And then if there's a payout, Then to me, that person's guilty. Why paying out if you have nothing to hide? And then we have a second bill coming up that simply says that the individual can sue because they're forced to go into this agreement that actually protects the congressman and and it doesn't protect the victim as well. And then also in my bill, if this complaint goes directly to the ethics committee and if there's evidence there that there's inappropriate contact that the person will be expelled from Congress.

explicit_propositions.text: It is outrageous that a congressperson has engaged in sexual misconduct toward a staff member.
The money used for payouts should come from the congressman’s personal funds, not taxpayer funds.
There is a legislative proposal requiring settlements to be funded by the congressman personally.
Some congresspeople have paid staff members off using tax dollars after allegations of sexual misconduct.
If the ethics committee finds evidence of misconduct, the congressperson should be expelled from Congress.
The ethics committee has the authority to investigate allegations of misconduct.
A congressional representative who pays a settlement should be publicly named.
This proposed legislation would apply retroactively to past cases.
If a payout occurs, the congressman is presumed guilty.
Another bill is being introduced allowing victims to sue due to coercive settlement agreements.

assumptions.text: Financial responsibility for wrongdoing should fall on the individual perpetrator, not the public.
Public naming of individuals accused of misconduct serves as a deterrent and promotes accountability.
Coercive settlement agreements inherently disadvantage victims and shield perpetrators.
Expulsion from Congress is an appropriate consequence for proven misconduct.
Presumption of guilt upon payment reflects reasonable inference based on behavior.
Victims deserve legal recourse independent of institutional processes.
Taxpayer-funded settlements undermine public trust in government institutions.
Retrospective application of laws is ethically justified when addressing serious harm.
Congressional ethics committees are capable and credible bodies for investigating misconduct.
The existence of a formal process like an ethics committee justifies public disclosure of findings.
